Hello! I'm a master's student at the University of Bonn working in formalization. As part of my master's thesis, I'd like to be working on Turing machines, computability and in particular NP-completeness. I previously worked on a project aiming to formalize Cook's theorem (just based on mathlib and available at https://git.abstractnonsen.se/max/mathlib4, see https://git.abstractnonsen.se/max/mathlib4/src/commit/0f4c50edbe7ac8b5f92fee9f514b4385446c4bd6/Mathlib/Computability/Cook.lean#L1231 for the main result of the project, which is essentially the "hard" part of the proof of Cook's theorem).

My advisor and I were thinking that CSLib would be the natural place to contribute such a formalization to, and thus I wanted to talk with the maintainer team about the library's plans on this topic (so that ideally, things would align with the library's development process).
As far as I can see, CSLib does not have a lot of Turing machines formalized yet (there is a SingleTapeTM, and a PR for a MultiTapeTM as far as I can see). Compared to that, Mathlib has some things as well (which I have worked with for my project), but it's also not very far and the mathlib mainline isn't oriented towards tracking polynomial-time equivalence of equations.

Regarding future work, there are the following questions that I would like to be talking about:

  • Would such a contribution, generally targeted towards Cook's theorem (and developing various prerequisites needed to formulate it etc) be welcome in CSLib?
  • Are there existing theoretical guidelines / concepts on how (Turing-)computability is meant to be formalized in CSLib?
  • In my (albeit limited) experience, a big challenge in tackling the full scope of this theorem / Turing computability in general is that it is hard to prove the existence of specific Turing machines and the functions that they compute, even basic ones, since programming on them is cumbersome. Are the existing plans on developing some kind of higher-level programming language (or formalizing an existing one) in a suitable computation model + showing polynomial-time equivalence to the turing model? Such a machinery would be hardish to build up, but very convenient in formalizing lots of theorems later on when developing the theory. In principle, I would be interested on working on that (if it does not exist already).
  • Who are the people I should talk to about this, e.g., are there people already working on such or similar topics in CSLib?

Right now, I'm generally just looking to get in touch with the relevant people in order to discuss ideas and details about such a project and how to integrate it into CSLib.
Thank you all for your help and interest.
@Fabrizio Montesi

Formalizing the theory of NP-completeness is very much within the scope of CSLib. I know that a couple of people are working on the Turing machine, e.g., Christian Reitwiessner (see also his talk). He had a DSL for a Turing machine.

I never work on TM myself, but I am happy to coordinate the contribution to CSLib. There is no official guideline for how a Turing machine should be formalized, but we would love to discuss that here. The first step is to propose definitions and state the theorems, and then you can propose the plan to carry out the PR. Then we can see if experts agree on them.
I would also suggest that we create a working group for this topic if there are enough people working on it.

Hi Maximilian! I can’t speak for what are the plans for cslib, but I’m working on formalizing complexity theory and in particular sub-linear space complexity. I have some PRs to cslib, but the bulk of my work is at https://github.com/crei/cslib . The core is a set of tools to specify Turing machines. One example is a TM that verifies a cnf formula: https://github.com/crei/cslib/blob/53ce1343ac8ae1a0c1dca2c466ea77b1018ce846/Cslib/Computability/Machines/MultiTapeTuring/Satisfiability.lean#L203 I think this “language” is not too difficult to “program” in and at the same time it stays close to the TM model to allow tight time and space bounds. I’m also happy to have a call about this topic if you want!
Just as a heads up, a group of complexity theory researchers and I are already working on this.

We plan to go beyond cook-levin of course, but cook levin would be a welcome addition. This work is happening in Algolean which we intend to keep as a library for TCS researchers in synch with CSLib. We are also happy to coordinate on NP completeness reductions. I am in the process of adding these definitions after fixing some existing definitions. Happy to coordinate efforts on any other related topics, including uniform circuit complexity.

Like @Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai already wrote, Cook–Levin would be very welcome, as well as all the building blocks leading up to it.

It'd be great to start by discussing on this Zulip the missing components needed in a bit more detail. Please keep an eye also on the open PRs about TMs: https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pulls?q=is%3Apr+is%3Aopen+turing

I'd be very interested in talking about a compositional language that is defined directly on or compiled to TMs.

@Fabrizio Montesi I already have one example of such a language. After some fixes, I should be able to state definitions for P and NP for any model polytime reducible to TMs. Happy to learn about alternatives. This is a space where a lot of PL people might have done interesting work, for example cbpv lambda calculus.
If we're just interested in complexity classes, one might not even need TMs and use a calculus directly, e.g., https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.3311
(I mean for this specific problem, in general of course that's not all we're interested in.)

You might also be interested in porting and extending this https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITP.2021.20

The only drawback so far is it might not work for fine grained complexity. But we need a word ram model for that anyway

Hey, thank you all for your replies, let me try to address some of the questions raised.

So far, I've only focused on time complexity up to a polynomial factor (which is all you need for Cook-Levin), and I based my work off mathlib (which has some slightly different definitions for Turing machines).
My existing work is to proof that for every verifier V of an NP-complete problem and any instance X, there is a SAT such that V accepts X for some certificate C if and only if the SAT is feasible. In some sense, this is the "hard" part of cook-levin, i.e. where the proof ideas go into. Looking at what is in CSLib and that the foundations are similar enough to mathlib, this could probably be ported to CSLib, which I'd be interested to do. To fully complete a proof of the theorem, you still need to show that this is a polynomial transformation, i.e. that converting an instance X into the corresponding SAT can be done in polynomial time by a turing machine.
This is the part where textbooks usually get handwavy since it's "obvious" that such TMs exist (we only care about polynomial time, so no sophisticated programming is required), but formalizing this without further preliminary work is difficult. Hence my interest in trying to build up some more high-level "programming" language or similar that would make it easier to prove the existence of such TMs. In particular, for such proofs (which appear in many classic NP reductions, for example the Karp ones), we do not really care about the actual Turing machine computing some functions, so proving polynomial-time equivalence of the comptuation model of Turing machines to some other model (for example, multi-tape TMs or RAMs etc) means it is sufficient to give polynomial-time algorithms on these models, which would likely be easier.

Fabrizio Montesi said:

I'd be very interested in talking about a compositional language that is defined directly on or compiled to TMs.

So yes, this is one of the things that I'd be interested to look at (the "compiled to") part, where we could develop (or choose an existing) a natural framework on where that compositional language lives.
In principle, this is the direction I would like to go with my future work, i.e. work on establishing polynomial-time equivalence to more complex models, which ultimately should yield a good basis for completing the cook-levin theorem.

@chris477 While I haven't checked it out fully, your work seems interesting and potentially related to what I'd be planning to do (as far as I can tell, you're also the author of the currently-pending PRs to CSLib regarding TMs), and I'd be happy to take you up on your offer for a call.

@Shreyas Srinivas Thanks for letting me know, I'll check out what algolean is doing as well and come back to you if I run into further questions regarding coordinating things.
The dagstuhl files seem interesting, in particular the choice of L as a foundation for time-complexity and carrying out reductions there by using the polynomial-time equivalence of computation to TMs.
I wasn't very concerned regarding fine-grained complexity thus far (simply because it wasn't the focus of my work), but maybe it's a good thing to have in mind long-term.

Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai said:

I would also suggest that we create a working group for this topic if there are enough people working on it.

I don't know how to do that, but it seems like a good idea. Would that also be the place where to start discussing more details (regarding missing components and what I'd be doing), or should that still happen in the discussion channel heres

Just to clarify @Maximilian Keßler I am already approaching these model agnostic definitions (upto polytime reduction to TMs). I just need to introduce the definition of a config trace of a turing machine and rewrite complexity classes in terms of them.

@Shreyas Srinivas Okay, good to know. Previously, I worked with these definitions (see https://git.abstractnonsen.se/max/mathlib4/src/commit/0f4c50edbe7ac8b5f92fee9f514b4385446c4bd6/Mathlib/Computability/TMComputableBase.lean#L23-L31 for context):

/-- Bundle of a type `σ` with a step function `σ → Option σ`. -/
class TMBase (τ : Type*) where
      σ (a : τ) : Type
      step {a : τ} : σ a → Option (σ a)

/-- An abstract version of a turing machine with input alphabet `Γ₀` and output alphabet `Γ₁`. -/
class TM (τ : Type*) (Γ₀ Γ₁ : Type) extends TMBase τ where
      init {a : τ} : List Γ₀ → σ a
      output {a : τ}: σ a → List Γ₁

and built the general definitions on top of that, then defined how each specific TM model fits into this abstract view. Out of curiosity: Is this similar to what you are working on when you're talking about model agnostic definitions?

I think what you are doing is closer in principle to TM2Computable:
https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/25a4a334cf5211f694a9d798ed78d2c696f3661f/Mathlib/Computability/TuringMachine/Computable.lean#L155-L162

Hey @Maximilian Keßler how is progress going on this? I was thinking of trying to add "roadmap" for complexity theory including the cook-levin theorem to this recently announced AI driven Tau Ceti project (#Project announcements > Tau Ceti ). My thinking was that the common issue I often see with formalizing TM-based complexity theory is you have to make lots of machines for simple tasks, and perhaps it could be possible to set things up so that an AI could handle all these low-level tasks, making it easier to finish the high-level result.

I've had a roadmap written up for complexity in https://github.com/SamuelSchlesinger/complexitylib that I've had Claude and Codex chewing on for a while, I have Cook-Levin and BPP subseteq P/poly and all sorts of other nice things.

The answer is: yes, the AI can do lots of these things autonomously and indeed it writes tons of little TMs. I tried to encourage it to be composable in various ways, but it can only go so far with TMs.
The codebase is kinda enormous at this point, almost 300k lines of code.

I think at some point we have to deviate from Turing machines and also have theorems of the form "this class of functions can be computed in this time and space" plus composition theorems, and I think we can get quite far with this. Boolean negation is "regular" and thus in constant space and linear time. Also the complexity of identifying an element from a list could be done using composition etc. The hard part for me is always ignoring my default thought pattern of finding an algorithm that performs well in practice instead of finding a simple one that might have a 10-times overhead.

The point where this gets tricky is recursion. I tried to prove Savitch's theorem (which requires double recursion) using Turing machines and got utterly stuck. Because of that, I built a higher-level language, a fragment of which maps directly to Turing machines here: https://github.com/crei/cslib/pull/175

The idea (not yet fully executed) is to map the full language (which has higher-order functions) to the fragment and then we would have a language that allows to write complicated algorithm but also preserves time and space guarantees in exactly the way complexity proofs require (linear space and polynomial time).

Another nice aspect about that language is that it works on a data structure

inductive Data where | l : List Data → Data

which can be easily encoded into a boolean alphabet using parentheses but at the same time virtually any lean type can encode "directly" into it, so it is very easy to translate lean functions into this language.

I wasn't able to get much feedback yet on this design, so any comment is greatly appreciated!

Hey, getting back to this now:
I agree that the "hard part" of formalizing complexity theory is often that you need to give TMs for simple tasks, which is cumbersome to do manually, and I understand to use AI for doing such tedious but mathematically less uninsightful parts.
Personally, I do not wish to go that route. My goal is to build a more general approach to computability theory by first building bridges between TMS and other computation models (my next goal would be λ-calculus). Then, develop some small/easy (probably functional) programming language to sit on top of that that allows us to make the existence proofs of computable functions much more accessible in the long run. Then, we can skip over specifying and reasoning about TMS manually completely, and also don't need an AI to do this.

As to update on the current status of the project: I have completed the equivalence part of cook-levin, that is, show that for any instance of any NP problem, you can build a SAT-formula for that instance that is satisfiable if and only if there is a valid accepting certificate for the NP-problem.
It remains to be shown that this SAT is computable in poly-time depending on the instance, and that SAT itself is an NP-problem to finish cook-levin. Both of these boil down to existence proofs of computability of certain functions and are "obvious" in spirit why such a function exists.
Hence me focusing on building more foundations that will (hopefully) allow us to make this easier.

I agree that at some point we need to deviate from turing machines, which I'll also be trying to do. What is your goal of this higher-level language? Is it meant to "compile to" Turing machines and make it easier to specify them? Do you think Savitch's theorem would be more accessible if you were to work with some other model than TMs?

The language has its own semantics and resource consumption model. It's similar to lambda calculus but also has constructors and eliminators for Data plus while loops. For a fragment of that language where no variables are captured, the language can be directly simulated by a TM in a way where the TM uses one tape per node in the expression tree. It is space-reasonable (above linear) because the while loop body can re-use tapes.
Now the core idea is that you can use this fragment to de-functionalize the full language - I think a direct approach using TMs to simulate a higher-order language would be very hard.
Once you have that, I think that savitch is much easier. If you do it directly with TMs you again have to reason about stack and recursion, etc, (almost) the whole mechanism that we used for de-functionalization, just for the specific case of savitch alone.

Worth noting that Open AI's recent GapCVP result included "incidentally" a proof of Cook's theorem, specifically that 3-SAT is NP-hard. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/ten-proofs/refs/heads/main/GapCVP.lean

I figured they would necessarily include that fact, since the whole GapCVP result is about Turing machines. But I couldn't find it for the life of me in this massive file. Claude could!

Line 88642: theorem paperOriginalThreeSATIsNPHard.
Oh interesting, I hadn’t realized that! What kind of reduction notion did they use? Polynomial-time-many-one?

Yes:

abbrev BitLanguage := List Bool → Bool

abbrev VerifierTM (verifier : List Bool × List Bool → Bool) :=
  Turing.TM2ComputableInPolyTime
    pairBitEncoding Computability.encodeBool verifier

noncomputable def IsNP (L : BitLanguage) : Bool :=
  @decide (
  ∃ (bound : Polynomial ℕ) (verifier : List Bool × List Bool → Bool),
    Nonempty (VerifierTM verifier) ∧
      ∀ x : List Bool,
        L x ↔ ∃ certificate : List Bool,
          certificate.length ≤ bound.eval x.length ∧
            verifier (x, certificate) = true
  ) (Classical.propDecidable _)

structure PolynomialReduction (A B : BitLanguage) where
  map : List Bool → List Bool
  polynomial_time : Nonempty
    (BitTM map)
  correct : ∀ x, A x ↔ B (map x)

noncomputable def NPHard (L : BitLanguage) : Bool :=
  @decide (
  ∀ A : BitLanguage, IsNP A → Nonempty (PolynomialReduction A L)
  ) (Classical.propDecidable _)

Definitely a bit odd to write it as Bool with @decide and Classical.propDecidable ... but I can't call it wrong!
